references.docstring:
Reveal the rectangular patch hidden by the solid marker using the grid's reflection symmetries.

Input structure:
- A square colored pattern with one solid rectangular marker color occluding a patch.
- The visible pattern has horizontal and vertical reflection symmetry on a large lower/right strip.
- The top and left outer strips also expose transpose counterparts for cells not recoverable by those reflections.

Rule:
- Find the unique color whose full extent is a solid rectangle; this rectangle is the output region.
- Infer the reflected strip start as the smallest row/column offset whose lower/right strips are mirror-consistent, ignoring marker pixels.
- For each marker pixel, copy the unique non-marker value in its horizontal/vertical reflection orbit; if that orbit is entirely hidden in the outer strip, use the transposed top/left-strip counterpart.

Key insight:
The marker is not part of the pattern; it covers a missing rectangle whose cells are still determined by the visible mirror or transpose copies elsewhere in the grid.

annotation.src: solid rectangular marker over a mirrored color pattern
annotation.dst: hidden marker-sized rectangle
annotation.transform: replace each marker pixel by the matching pixel from its horizontal/vertical reflection orbit; use the transposed top/left-strip counterpart when that orbit is also hidden
annotation.grid_shape: crop to marker bbox

references.docstring:
Repair noisy periodic patterns inside frame-delimited grid regions.

Input structure:
- Frame color (most common) forms full rows/cols, dividing the grid into rectangular regions.
- bg (second most common) fills empty space; each region contains a small colored tile repeated periodically with a few corrupted pixels.

Rule:
- For each region, find the bounding box of non-bg content.
- Infer the smallest repeating tile that explains the pattern (majority vote per residue position), requiring it repeat at least 2x per axis.
- Replace the region with the clean tiled version.

Key insight: Tile dimensions are unknown and must be inferred; prefer the smallest tile with genuine repetition over one that memorizes the entire region.

Draw a polyline by decoding 3x3 glyph instructions read across a divided grid.

Input structure:
- Left of a full-height vertical divider: 3x3 colored glyphs on bg.
- Right of divider: a single gray (5) start pixel.

Rule:
- Remove the divider; shift the gray start into the left canvas.
- Read glyphs in column-major order (left→right, top→bottom).
- Each glyph's shape (pixel area) encodes a segment: area 4 → down 2, area 5 → right 3, area 6 → left 4, area 7 → left 2.
- Append segments sequentially, stepping down one cell between each.

Key insight: Glyph pixel count (area) uniquely determines both segment length and direction — the shape itself is the instruction.

annotation.src: 3x3 glyphs left of a vertical divider, plus a gray start marker on the right
annotation.dst: a single polyline in the left canvas starting at the shifted gray marker
annotation.match_cond: glyphs ordered by tile column (left→right), then tile row (top→bottom)
annotation.transform: remove divider, shift gray into the left canvas, then append one segment per glyph while moving downward; segment length+orientation are determined by glyph type (area 4→vertical len2; area 5→horizontal len3 right; area 6→horizontal len4 left; area 7→horizontal len2 left)

references.docstring:
Fill partitioned regions with concentric colored bands derived from marker pixels.

Input structure:
- Grid partitioned into regions by wall-colored lines.
- Each region has a dominant base color and a few isolated marker pixels of other colors at varying depths from the region boundary.

Rule:
- For each region, read marker colors ordered by their Chebyshev distance from the boundary to build a color palette.
- If no marker sits on the boundary itself, the base color leads the palette.
- Paint every cell with palette[distance mod palette_length], producing repeating concentric rectangular frames that radiate inward.

Key insight: Each marker's depth from the boundary defines its position in the cyclic palette; the pattern then tiles inward automatically.

annotation.summary: Isolated colored pixels in each region expand by drawing alternating concentric rectangular frames parallel to region boundaries until the entire region is filled.
annotation.src: isolated single colored pixels within each partitioned region s
annotation.path: draw rectangular frame parallel to region boundary, then shrink inward by 1 pixel and repeat alternating s.color with background until region is filled
annotation.trajectory: paint s.color on current frame, alternate with region background color on next frame, continue inward

references.docstring:
Trace diagonal rays from triangular arrows, reflecting off colored wall pixels.

Input structure:
- bg grid with monochrome 3-pixel L-shaped "arrows" (2x2 bbox missing one corner) and scattered colored wall pixels.

Rule:
- Each arrow fires a ray diagonally away from its missing corner, painting bg cells in its color.
- A head-on wall hit reverses both axes; a side-touch wall hit flips the touched axis only.
- On any bounce the ray adopts the wall's color and recolors the contact cell.
- Ray stops when it exits the grid or reaches another arrow.

Key insight: Two distinct reflection types (corner vs side-touch) plus color inheritance at each bounce drive the path geometry.

annotation.src: triangular arrow
annotation.path: along the diagonal line pointed by the arrow then reflected by the wall
annotation.trajectory: continuous; ray color changes to wall color on each reflection
annotation.dst: out of grid
annotation.multi_step: reflected by all reachable walls one by one

references.docstring:
Assemble colored sprites into a central bar's notches, chaining successive pieces along fixed-width strips.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Largest monochrome component is a solid "bar" with boundary notches (bg holes opening to its bbox edge).
- Several smaller colored sprites scattered around the bar.

Rule:
- Each bar notch is filled by a root piece whose shape exactly covers the hole.
- The root defines a strip (column-span or row-span) for its chain.
- Successive pieces fill the bg cells inside the previous piece's bbox, locked to the same strip width.
- Multiple chains grow independently from different bar notches.

Key insight: The root piece's extent perpendicular to the chain direction locks the strip width for all subsequent pieces in that chain.

annotation.src: dangling monochrome sprite s
annotation.dst: plug into central bar or previously plugged sprite d
annotation.match_cond: s.shape fits into d.notch.shape
annotation.multi_step: place sprites one into the notch of another until no notches remain; multiple chains grow from different bar notches

references.docstring:
Fill periodic progressions that shoot from a unique grid edge.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.  Sparse non-bg dots of several colors.
- All repeating colors originate from the same grid edge (top, bottom,
  left, or right — the one with the most non-bg dots).
- Each repeating color has exactly 2 dots per shooting-direction line;
  their gap defines the step.
- Every non-bg dot lies on a shooting-direction line that contains a
  repeating color.

Rule:
- Determine the unique shooting edge; left/right → rows, top/bottom → columns.
- For each shooting-direction line, the repeating color has exactly 2 dots;
  step = gap between them, offset = first position mod step.
- A different-colored dot aligned to the same beat (pos % step == offset) is
  a companion: it absorbs the ray and becomes the fill color, limiting the
  fill range to the span between repeating and companion dots.
- An unaligned dot is a bystander and left untouched.
- Without a companion the repeating color fills the entire line.

Key insight: the shooting edge is identified by counting boundary dots;
the gap between the two marker dots is the period; a companion sharing the
modular class acts as a wall that stops the ray and dictates the paint color.

annotation.src: sparse colored dots
annotation.path: within each affected row/col, step size = gcd of gaps between repeated dots; traverse indices congruent to the first dot modulo step
annotation.trajectory: paint with the aligned companion color if present on the same modulo-class; otherwise paint with the dot color
annotation.dst: fill the line segment between extreme occurrences (or whole line if no companion color)
annotation.transform: fill background/marker cells on that path with the trajectory color; ties apply both row and column rules

references.docstring:
Detect thin '+' shapes in a single foreground color and recolor them to teal.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- One foreground color (e.g. yellow) forms various shapes on the bg, some of which are small '+' crosses.

Rule:
- A '+' center is any foreground pixel whose 4 orthogonal neighbors are also foreground.
- Recolor each such center and its 4 neighbors to teal (8).
- All other pixels remain unchanged.

Key insight: Only compact 5-cell crosses qualify — a pixel embedded in a larger filled region also satisfies the neighbor check, so the rule highlights every local '+' motif, not just isolated ones.

annotation.src: yellow plus sprites s
annotation.transform: s.color -> teal

references.docstring:
Simulate particles along a path with alternating turn direction at collisions.

Input structure:
- Top-left: 2x2 monochrome blocks define a repeating color cycle (left-to-right).
- Isolated single pixels of a cycle color: start markers adjacent to the path.
- A 2x2 monochrome block of a distinct color: end marker.

Rule:
- Each start marker launches a particle moving straight, painting cycle colors in order.
- On hitting a boundary, paint that cell with the end color and turn 90°.
- Turn direction alternates: odd collisions → left (CCW), even → right (CW).
- If the scheduled turn is blocked, the particle stops.

Key insight: The alternating left/right turn rule is the core mechanism; without it the path would be trivial.

annotation.src: start markers: isolated single pixels whose colors belong to a template cycle shown as 2x2 monochrome blocks in the top-left
annotation.path: enter the main path region (the most frequent non-template color) and move one cell per step; keep heading until a collision with non-path
annotation.trajectory: paint the path with a repeating color cycle (cycle order = 2x2 blocks left→right; advance cycle each step)
annotation.dst: stop when leaving the grid, or when the scheduled turn is blocked
annotation.transform: erase the template 2x2 blocks and the 2x2 end block; while moving, recolor visited path cells by the cycle; on collision into template background, paint that collided cell with the end-block color as a corner marker
annotation.turn_rule: CRUCIAL: collisions enforce strict alternating 90° turns: 1st/3rd/5th… turn left (CCW), 2nd/4th/6th… turn right (CW); if the scheduled turn cell is not path, STOP (no fallback)
annotation.notes: initial direction is the first adjacent path neighbor in priority R,D,L,U; cycle index starts at the marker’s own color within the cycle; apply independently for each marker

references.docstring:
Extend row bars periodically across the opposite side of a separator column.

Input structure:
- bg = background. A near-solid vertical separator divides the grid into two sides.
- One side contains horizontal colored bars; the other side is blank target space.
- Bars may be stacked by row and may sit at different distances from the separator.

Rule:
- Identify the separator as the column whose non-bg cells are one color.
- Treat the denser side as the bar side and collect each contiguous row run.
- Process bars from nearest to farthest from the separator; for each bar, paint its
  color every bar-length cells into the blank side without overwriting earlier paint.

Key insight: Each bar's length is the period for its extension, and nearer bars claim target cells first.

annotation.summary: Horizontal monochrome color bars to the left of a vertical separator bar extend rightward with periodic intervals equal to their pixel count.
annotation.src: horizontal monochrome color bars left of the vertical separator bar s
annotation.path: straight line from separator bar to the opposite grid edge, perpendicular to separator (rightward)
annotation.trajectory: paint s.color at intervals where interval = s.pixel_count
annotation.multi_step: Process multiple bars by distance from separator: start with the bar closest to the separator, then proceed outward; do not overwrite previously painted colors

references.docstring:
Connect two sprites using matching connector pixels, then tight-crop.

Input structure:
- Background color `bg`, sprite color `obj`, connector color `ctrl` (small, 2 components).
- Two main foreground sprites, plus possibly tiny detached pixels belonging to one sprite.

Rule:
- Identify the **base** sprite (closest to grid top-left).
- Translate the other sprite so its connector sits one cell above the base's connector.
- Stamp the plug onto the base; remove connectors (recolor `ctrl` to `obj`).
- Output is the tight crop around all non-background pixels.

Key insight: The connector pixels define the unique docking point and direction.

annotation.src: movable sprite with a connector
annotation.dst: plug into base sprite d in top-left corner with a connector
annotation.match_cond: s.connector.color/shape == d.connector.color/shape and s.connector above d.connector
annotation.src2: s.connector and d.connector
annotation.transform2: recolor connector pixels to body color
annotation.grid_shape: expand if needed then tight crop

references.docstring:
Repaint regions from T-shaped control markers, erase the markers, and optionally rotate based on a color-9 L-marker.

Input structure:
- The grid is a mosaic of monochrome regions.
- Color 1 forms T-shaped control markers on region boundaries.
- Some controls use three singleton color-1 pixels around a colored center; that center is a literal replacement color.
- An optional 5-cell L-shaped color-9 marker triggers 90-degree rotation of the output.

Rule:
- For a color-1 T marker, the single stem points at the destination region to repaint.
- The two diagonal cells behind the stem identify the source region; the destination gets that source region's original color.
- For a colored-center T marker, the same stem identifies the destination, but the center color is the replacement.
- All marker cells are filled with the final color of the source-side region.
- A 5-cell L-shaped color-9 marker controls rotation: ┐ (corner top-right) → CCW 90°, ┌ (corner top-left) → CW 90°.

Key insight:
- The stem chooses what changes, while the two diagonals behind the stem choose where the marker itself belongs.

annotation.src: monochrome regions with T-shaped color-1 control markers
annotation.transform: recolor the region pointed to by each T stem using the original color from the two diagonal source cells behind the stem; colored-center T markers use the center color instead; erase marker cells into the source-side region
annotation.grid_shape: same, except rotate 90 degrees when indicated by the colored-center control orientation
annotation.notes: small non-rectangular colored scraps are absorbed into the neighboring region

references.docstring:
Propagate a repeating striped pattern from a yellow border segment toward the opposite edge, recoloring foreground objects on certain stripes.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Foreground blobs of another color scattered in the interior.
- A short yellow (4) segment sits on one border edge.

Rule:
- From the yellow segment, march toward the opposite edge in steps of 2 cells, cycling colors Y, Y, G (4, 4, 3). The 1-cell gap between stripes is forced to bg.
- Yellow stripes paint only within the segment's span.
- Green stripes additionally recolor all non-bg pixels across the entire row/column to green.

Key insight: Green stripes act as a "flood" that recolors existing objects on the full row/column, while yellow stripes are confined to the segment span.

annotation.src: yellow line on edge
annotation.path: straight line
annotation.trajectory: YYGYYG...
annotation.dst: the opposite edge
annotation.src2: green line
annotation.path2: foreground pixels in the same row/col

references.docstring:
Move colored sprites from the left strip into a framed area at marker-defined targets.

Input structure:
- bg background; rectangular frame on right with colored markers on its edges; sprites in a narrow left strip separated by a constant-color divider column.

Rule:
- For each color, target rows/cols are where both opposite frame edges share that color. Targets are the Cartesian product.
- Erase each sprite from the left and stamp it centered at every target. Higher sprites cover lower ones.

Key insight: One sprite replicates to a grid of row × column marker intersections.

annotation.src: sprite s in the left area whose color appears on the right frame
annotation.dst: center at positions d in the right frame
annotation.match_cond: s.color == d.same_row_frame_edges.color and s.color == d.same_col_frame_edges.color
annotation.multi_step: move sprites from bottom to top, with new covering old

references.docstring:
Complete a visible crop into the shared 20x20 binary motif in its matching orientation.

Input structure:
- The grid is a two-color rectangular crop of one rotation/reflection of the same 20x20 motif.
- One color is the motif foreground and the other color is the motif background.

Rule:
- Try each input color as the foreground mask.
- Match that mask against every possible window in every dihedral orientation of the motif.
- Repaint the uniquely matched full 20x20 motif with the matched foreground/background colors.

Key insight:
- The examples are partial windows of one canonical binary pattern; the local crop is distinctive enough to identify the full orientation and offset.

annotation.src: visible two-color crop of a 20x20 binary motif
annotation.dst: the full 20x20 motif in the matching rotation/reflection and window position
annotation.transform: repaint the completed motif with the crop foreground color and background color

references.docstring:
Move bordered containers toward same-colored destination markers, charging gray cells to orange.

Input structure:
- bg = 6 (magenta). Black-bordered (0) rectangles with gray (5) / orange (7) interiors.
- A head sprite (9) sits adjacent to one container edge; a matching destination sprite lies along the movement axis.

Rule:
- Each container translates toward its destination along the head-to-dest axis.
- Steps = min(head-to-dest distance, number of gray interior cells).
- Gray cells become orange from the head-facing side inward, one per step.

Key insight: Gray cell count caps movement — a container stops short if it runs out of gray cells to charge.

annotation.src: rectangular container with head that has same color as destination line
annotation.path: head forward
annotation.dst: reach the destination line or move_distance == s.inner_gey_pixels.num
annotation.src2: inner grey pixels whose num == move_distance
annotation.transform: change color to orange
annotation.multi_step: grey pixels change color in order

references.docstring:
Simulate water pixels falling under gravity into basins formed by colored obstacles.

Input structure:
- bg = 0. Water pixels = color 1 (blue).
- Other colors form static solid structures (walls, steps, containers).
- Water starts in unstable positions above or beside basins.

Rule:
- Each water pixel falls straight down through bg cells.
- When blocked below, it slides diagonally through the unique open side cell.
- When resting on a surface, it slides horizontally toward the nearest gap where it can fall again.
- Process repeats until no water pixel moves.

Key insight: Water seeks the deepest reachable basin via diagonal and horizontal sliding, not just vertical fall.

annotation.src: blue pixels
annotation.path: flow along neighboring bg cells to left/right/down (like water)
annotation.dst: lowest postion possible (into basin)
annotation.multi_step: iteratively move blue pixels whose left or right side is bg

references.docstring:
Reorder and stack rectangles by proximity to two colored edge lines.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Two edge lines (h + v) meet at a corner marked by a unique color.
- "Blue" line is color 1 if present, else the longer line; other is "red."
- Solid rectangles in the interior.

Rule:
- Sort rectangles by (distance to blue edge, distance to red edge).
- If the blue edge is vertical, rotate each rectangle 90° CCW.
- Stack top-to-bottom, centered horizontally.

Key insight: Edge-line colors encode a coordinate system; proximity to each axis determines stacking order and rotation.

annotation.src: rectangles
annotation.dst: into slot center aligned
annotation.match_cond: (distance(s, blue_edge), distance(s, red_edge)).order == d.pos.row.order
annotation.transform: rot90 if blue edge is vertical
annotation.multi_step: move rectangles in order, one below another

references.docstring:
Simulate tokens falling through a pipe network after gates rotate open.

Input structure:
- Wall (0), bg (pipe fill), gate (horizontal 1×3 bars), token (small edge pixels).

Rule:
- Rotate each gate into a vertical blocker; gate cells become bg.
- Tokens drop downward through bg, choosing the extreme column for their side (left→min, right→max).
- Tokens settle at true pipe ends (adjacent to wall/boundary), packing inward.

Key insight: Tokens select drop columns by entry side and land at wall-bounded endpoints, ignoring blocker-bounded ones.

annotation.src: 3x3 square with orange horizontal bar in middel row
annotation.transform: rot90, orange bar change to magenta
annotation.src2: green pixel
annotation.dst2: endpoint of path next to grid edge
annotation.multi_step: rotate_in_place then move_along_path

references.docstring:
Sort scattered 4×4 squares into two columns by type: frames left, solids right.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Multiple 4×4 objects on bg.
- Frames: colored 1px border, bg-filled 2×2 interior.
- Solids: entirely filled with one non-bg color.

Rule:
- Classify each 4×4 object as frame or solid by its interior.
- Sort each group top-to-bottom by input row.
- Stack frames in left column (cols 0–3), solids in right (cols 4–7).
- Output is 8 wide; height = 4 × max(#frames, #solids), bg-padded.

Key insight: Frame vs solid is determined solely by whether the 2×2 interior matches bg.

annotation.src: hollow square
annotation.dst: into left slot
annotation.match_cond: s.pos.row.order == d.pos.row.order
annotation.src2: solid square
annotation.multi_step: move squares from top to bottom, then from left to right

references.docstring:
Attach monochrome sprites to the matching sides of a central hollow square.

Input structure:
- bg = background. A hollow NxN square (hub) with bg corners/interior and four differently-colored edges (top, bottom, left, right).
- 2-4 monochrome sprites scattered on the grid, each matching one hub edge color.

Rule:
- For each hub edge color, find the matching sprite outside the hub.
- Rotate the sprite (0/90/180/270°) so its contact edge has exactly N-2 contiguous cells aligned with the hub side, and the rotated sprite is mirror-symmetric along the contact-edge axis (UD for left/right, LR for top/bottom).
- Translate it to adjoin that hub side. 
- Clear everything else to bg; output is hub + attached sprites only.

Key insight: Each edge color uniquely pairs a sprite to a side; symmetry along the contact-edge axis disambiguates the correct rotation.

annotation.src: solid monochrome sprite s
annotation.dst: attach to an edge of hollow polychrome sprite d with bg corners and 4 differently-colored side edges
annotation.match_cond: s.head.color == d.edge.color and s.head.length == d.edge.length
annotation.transform: rotate s to align matching edge with d.side

references.docstring:
Convert a rough nested line drawing into a clean canonical frame-and-dot diagram.

Input structure:
- The grid has one background color and one foreground color.
- Foreground 4-connected objects are rough closed frames or small filled blobs.
- Frames may contain other frames/blobs; blobs outside a frame remain outside it.

Rule:
- Detect the containment tree of foreground objects using holes of each frame object.
- Replace every blob with one foreground pixel.
- Replace every frame with a rectangular border padded two cells around its direct children.
- Place siblings by their original row/column overlap and order, with one empty cell between canonical objects.

Key insight: The exact wobbly geometry is irrelevant; only enclosure plus relative sibling positions define the output.

annotation.src: rough two-color nested foreground drawing: closed frame objects and small blob objects
annotation.dst: canonical frame-and-dot diagram preserving containment and sibling row/column order
annotation.transform: replace each blob by one pixel; replace each frame by a rectangular border padded around its direct children; keep outside blobs outside the enclosing frame
annotation.grid_shape: canonical crop; root-level outside blobs occupy a 3x3 bg slot

references.docstring:
Sort vertical bars by height and redistribute them across fixed colored slots.

Input structure:
- bg background; a horizontal base line of a single color spans the full grid width.
- Several monochrome vertical bars of distinct colors rise upward from the base line.

Rule:
- Rank bar shapes by height (shortest to tallest).
- Rank original x-positions (slots) left to right.
- Place the i-th shortest shape into the i-th leftmost slot, recoloring it to that slot's original color.
- The base line is preserved unchanged.

Key insight: Each slot keeps its x-position and color identity; only the bar silhouettes are redistributed among slots by height order.

annotation.src: vertical bar sprite s
annotation.dst: replace vertical bar d
annotation.match_cond: s.size.order == d.pos.col.order
annotation.transform: s.color -> d.color

references.docstring:
Slide a solid square through a winding channel to reach a same-sized target square.

Input structure:
- bg (most common color). A river color forms a winding corridor.
- Two same-sized NxN solid squares on the river: mover and destination, each a distinct color.

Rule:
- The mover square travels along the river toward the destination.
- It can only pass through positions where the full NxN area is river.
- If reachable, the mover replaces the destination; otherwise it stops at the farthest reachable point.
- The mover's original position is filled with the river color.

Key insight: Chokepoints narrower than N pixels block the square, forcing it to stop short.

annotation.src: black square
annotation.path: blue pixels "water channel" that is wide enough to pass through until "stuck" because of too narrow
annotation.dst: reach same sized red square or "get stuck" on the way where the blue path is too narrow
annotation.transform: cover the red square if reaching it

references.docstring:
Complete outlined shapes and carry attached shadow pixels along their edges.

Input structure:
- bg = background. Each active color marks vertices of an 8-direction aligned outline.
- A start vertex can have adjacent non-bg, different-colored shadow pixels.
- Other colored pixels may be distractors unless they lie on valid drawable edges.

Rule:
- For each color, order its pixels by polar angle around their centroid to form a cycle.
- Draw only horizontal, vertical, or 45-degree edges whose interiors are clear.
- From the chosen start vertex, copy adjacent shadow offsets along each drawable edge
  when the parallel path is in bounds and clear.

Key insight: The main outline is reconstructed first, then the start vertex's neighbor offsets define parallel shadow strokes.

annotation.summary: Connect same-colored pixels along horizontal, vertical, or 45/135-degree diagonal paths, with neighbor pixels from the starting point following in parallel offset positions.
annotation.src: pairs of same-colored pixels s
annotation.match_cond: s1.color == s2.color
annotation.path: connect s1 to s2 along horizontal, vertical, or strict 45/135-degree diagonal line
annotation.trajectory: paint s.color along entire path between same-colored pixels
annotation.multi_step: Step 1: identify pairs of same-colored pixels that can connect via H/V/diagonal; Step 2: draw connecting line between them; Step 3: for each neighbor of starting pixel, draw parallel line with same offset
annotation.src2: neighbor pixels in 8-connected neighborhood of path starting point s
annotation.path2: parallel to primary path, offset by relative position of neighbor to starting pixel

references.docstring:
Simulate water falling from top-edge sources, pooling on shelves, and cascading off edges.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color; water = rarest non-bg; shelf = other non-bg.
- Sources: water clusters touching top row. Shelves: horizontal segments.

Rule:
- Water falls down from sources, painting bg cells as water.
- On hitting a shelf, it spreads across the shelf span plus one cell past each end.
- From those overflow positions, water resumes falling independently.

Key insight: Each shelf splits a stream into two at its edges, creating a branching waterfall tree.

annotation.src: vertical magenta bar (liquid flow) from top edge of grid
annotation.path: through orange bg (air), vertical down or horizontal to both sides when landing on red horizontal bar
annotation.dst: bottom edge of grid
annotation.trajectory: continuous
annotation.multi_step: alternate vertical and horizontal movements until reaching bottom edge

references.docstring:
Extract the unique cell from each lattice row into a single-column lattice.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into equal square cells by uniform gridlines of color L.
- Cell interiors filled with bg; each cell has an inner sprite pattern.
- Each row of cells has exactly one cell with a unique pattern; the rest are copies.

Rule:
- For each lattice row, find the cell whose inner pattern appears exactly once (the "odd one out").
- Construct a single-column lattice preserving the original row heights, containing only the unique cells.

Key insight: The task is per-row "odd one out" — every cell in a row is identical except one oddball, which must be extracted.

annotation.src: square s with a unique inner sprite in its row
annotation.dst: place into slot d in a column of slots
annotation.match_cond: s.pos.row == d.pos.row
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop

references.docstring:
Fill holes in a target object with colors from a source object's subsprites, then tight-crop.

Input structure:
- bg = background. Two similar 8-connected objects share an outline color.
- Source has colored subsprites in cavities; target has empty cavities.

Rule:
- Find the two 8-connected objects.
- Target = object with more hole area. Align subsprites to holes (rotation/flip if needed).
- Fill each hole with its matched subsprite color; tight-crop.

Key insight: Hole centers in the target are matched to source subsprite centers under the best rotation/flip transform.

annotation.src: sprite s with colored inner subsprites
annotation.dst: merge with sprite d with holes
annotation.match_cond: s.subsprites.arrangement == d.holes.arrangement
annotation.transform: fill each hole in d with color of corresponding subsprite in s
annotation.grid_shape: tight crop

references.docstring:
Eject content pixels from cup-shaped frames outward along each cup's tail direction.

Input structure:
- bg = background. Hollow cup/Y/funnel frames, each a unique border color.
- Each cup has a convergent tail spike on one side and an open mouth on the opposite side.
- Content pixels (a single non-border color per cup) sit inside the cup's mouth interior.

Rule:
- For each cup, identify its tail spike and tail direction.
- Erase all content pixels from the mouth interior.
- Draw a straight line of content-colored pixels from the spike outward in the tail direction,
  one pixel per erased content pixel; cells beyond the grid edge are dropped.

Key insight: The tail spike is the unique convergent point whose outward direction is opposite
the mouth opening where the content lives.

annotation.src: colored pixels in the "mouth" of "Y-shaped" sprite
annotation.path: straight line in direction pointed by the convex part (tail) on the other side of the same "Y-shaped" sprite
annotation.dst: stack onto tail or onto other colored pixels already stacked
annotation.trajectory: ignore colored pixels stacked out of grid
annotation.src2: colored pixels not in the "mouth" of "Y-shaped" sprite
annotation.multi_step: move orange pixels to sprite tail one by one

references.docstring:

- Start at the square matching first control color c0.
- For each consecutive pair (ci, ci+1), find the ci+1-colored square aligned in the same row or column band, preferring nearest.
- Draw a bridge colored ci between the pair, spanning the gap with inner-square thickness.

references.docstring:
Fire projectiles from 3-pixel triangle sprites; mark collisions with maroon or blue.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. Non-bg 3-pixel sprites shaped as axis-aligned L's or diagonal V's.

Rule:
- Each triangle has an apex and an emission direction determined by its shape: L-shapes fire diagonally away from the missing corner; V-shapes fire along the axis away from the open side.
- A projectile lands exactly 5 cells from the apex in the emission direction.
- If it hits an existing sprite, that entire sprite is recolored to maroon (9).
- If two projectiles land on the same empty cell, that cell becomes blue (1); a lone projectile on empty bg paints maroon (9).

Key insight: The triangle's orientation encodes both direction and target; dual-projectile collisions on open bg produce blue, not maroon.

Fit a grey bar into a grey frame by aligning projections with colored columns, then stack colors above.

references.docstring:
Replicate a pre-drawn corner pattern to every other marker-bearing corner.

Input structure:
- bg = most frequent color. Hollow 0-frames (possibly partial L-shapes); each

  cells and an inward-diagonal trail).
- Other corners: a single colored pixel on the inward diagonal at the pattern's
  deepest (k,k) offset; the pixel's color is that corner's target color.

Rule:
- Extract the canonical (TL-oriented) pattern from any source.
- For each non-source corner whose marker cell is colored, paint the same
  pattern rotated to that corner's orientation, using the marker's color.

Key insight: the pattern is symmetric about the corner's inward-diagonal axis
(canonical dr == dc), so it reflects cleanly across all four corner orientations.
Painting uses each target's OWN marker color, not the source color.

- Two frames form a training pair (their interiors share the same color palette); one remaining frame is the test case.

Rule:
- Identify the training pair by matching interior color sets; the other non-blank frame is the test input.
- Infer the rule mapping source→destination (e.g. reflection, color inversion, gap filling, endpoint extraction, or checkerboard complement).
- Apply that same rule to the test sprite; output the transformed interior.

Key insight: The puzzle is an analogy — "A is to B as C is to ?" — where you must discover the visual rule from one example pair and generalize it.

references.docstring:
Move a triangular sprite across the grid, consuming aligned marker pixels.

Input structure:
- Frames concatenated horizontally with solid divider columns; bg is most common color.

- On reaching a marker, consume it; sprite re-faces that direction.
- Repeat until no markers remain; output the final sprite position on a clean bg.

Key insight: The triangle's tip encodes facing direction, which sets marker-consumption priority.

references.docstring:
Slide multi-color sprites to align their marker pixels with matching isolated border anchors.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Multi-color sprites in the interior; each has a minority-color "marker" pixel.
- Isolated border pixels (non-bg with all 4-neighbors bg) act as anchors.

Rule:
- Match each sprite to the border anchor sharing its marker color.
- Top/bottom-edge anchor (non-corner): slide sprite horizontally so marker column = anchor column.
- Left/right-edge anchor (or corner): slide sprite vertically so marker row = anchor row.

Key insight: The anchor's edge position determines the slide axis — top/bottom means horizontal, left/right (or corner) means vertical.

references.docstring:
Count colored objects and record tallies inside a legend box.

Input structure:
- A black rectangular legend box with key-color pixels in its leftmost non-black column.
- Outside the box, distinct objects of each key color are scattered across the grid.

- For each key color, count separate same-colored objects outside the legend box.
- Output the legend box repainted: each key row gets one dot per object, spaced every other cell rightward from the key pixel.

Key insight: The legend is both the color index and the output canvas — object counts become dot sequences on the matching row.

references.docstring:
Carve color-matched motifs into solid blocks and pack them into a compact grid.

references.docstring:
Build a red ray network by activating blue blobs via directional green ports.

- bg = most common color. Large blue blobs with adjacent green pixels marking port directions.

- Extend a ray upward from start; on hitting a blue blob, recolor it red.

references.docstring:
Fill rectangular cavities in a template shape by placing source sprites into matching holes.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color. A dominant "base" color forms a large frame/template with rectangular gaps.
- Small colored sprites sit outside the template region.

- The base color (largest connected component excluding bg) defines the template bbox.
- Each rectangular hole inside the template matches exactly one outside sprite by size.
- Place each sprite into its matching cavity; output is the filled template bbox.

references.docstring:
Sort objects to top or bottom edge by whether their shape (up to rotation/flip) is shared.

Input structure:
- bg = most common color.
- Several multicolor connected components (8-connected) scattered across the grid.

Rule:
- Compute each object's canonical shape (binary mask, invariant to rotation and flip).
- Objects whose shape appears in two or more components → translate to TOP edge (row 0).
- Objects whose shape is unique → translate to BOTTOM edge (row H−h).
- Horizontal position (left column) is preserved; only vertical translation changes.

Key insight: The sorting criterion is shape frequency (rotation-invariant), not area — duplicated shapes go up, unique shapes go down.

Copy colored control-ray ports from one rectangular sprite orientation to every matching transformed sprite.

Input structure:
- bg is the most common color.
- Several dense 2-by-N or N-by-2 rectangular sprites are dihedral transforms of one template.
- Isolated single-pixel control markers sit on rays projected outward from the dominant long edge of some sprites.

Rule:
- For each sprite, the active edge is the long side whose cells have the strongest same-color majority.
- A control marker seen first along an outward ray from an active-edge cell assigns its color to that template cell.
- On every transformed sprite, draw that assigned color outward from the corresponding active-edge cell through bg cells until blocked or out of bounds.

Key insight:
- The marker positions are not absolute; they label cells of a shared rectangular template, then the labels follow each sprite's rotation/reflection.

references.docstring:
Decode a stamp map: read templates, markers, and palette from a tiled grid, then render stamps.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into K tile columns (each N wide) separated by 1-col dashed separators.
- Top band (rows 0..N-1): K template masks, one per tile column.
- Middle band (rows N+1..2N): marker pixels whose color picks a template.
- Bottom band (rows 2N+2..): K palette swatches giving the output color per template.
- Separator rows at rows N and 2N+1 (dashed pattern of sep color).

Rule:
- Each marker's local position (lr, lc) within its tile column determines which N×N output block to stamp.
- The marker's color identifies which template to use; the palette recolors the template.

Key insight: Marker color encodes template index; local position within tile column encodes stamp block.

- Outside the frame: small monochrome sprites scattered on bg.

- Crop to the frame's bounding box; fill entirely with frame color.
- For each hole, find an outside sprite whose shape matches (rotation/flip allowed).
- Fill the hole with the matched sprite's color. If multiple sprites match, use the most frequent color.

Key insight: Sprites act as shape-coded color keys — their shape identifies which hole they fill, their color determines the fill color.

Input structure:
- bg; colored stripes (edge + internal) partition grid into rectangular regions.

- Rotate/flip train so marker pixels face the same-color boundary stripe of the target region.
- Translate so couplers align exactly onto station cells; erase original position.

Crop a board cluster and rotate its color layers based on outside cue sprites.

- Tight-crop around the board cluster.
- For each color layer inside the crop, find its same-color cue outside.
- Rotate that layer clockwise by (cue pixel count mod 4) × 90°.

Fill the parallelogram-shaped region between parallel anti-diagonal line segments with red.

- bg = most common color.
- One non-bg color forms short diagonal segments, each lying on a single anti-diagonal (r+c = const).
- Segments come in parallel pairs bounding a region to be filled.

- For each main-diagonal axis (r−c = const), collect anti-diagonal segments whose span covers that axis.
- Sort those segments by their anti-diagonal index (r+c).
- Fill all bg cells lying strictly between consecutive segment pairs along that axis with red (color 2).

Key insight: The two diagonal directions decouple — segments sit on anti-diagonals, and filling sweeps along main diagonals between them, forming parallelogram regions.

Reorder 5×5 blocks into a connected strip by matching edge foreground pixels.

- bg = background; sep = divider color (full row/column lines).
- Several 5×5 sprite blocks in a grid, separated by sep lines.

Recolor a cropped template and repeat it according to a component-count stencil.

- Solid blue (1) separator rows or columns split the grid into four sections.

- Sections 3 and 4 are solid color swatches for output foreground and background.

- Crop section 1 to the bbox of its non-black pixels and recolor it with the two swatches.
- Count 4-connected non-black components in section 2.
- Repeat the recolored crop that many times, inserting one background-colored row/column between copies.

is inherited from whether the input separators are columns or rows.

references.docstring:
Replicate a motif across quadrants with scaling and reflection keyed to red anchor blocks.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into four quadrants by a full-row and full-column divider of a single non-bg color.
- Each quadrant contains a red (2) square anchor block of varying size.
- The top-left quadrant also has a colored motif attached to its red anchor.

- Use the top-left quadrant's motif as the source pattern.
- For each other quadrant, scale the motif by the ratio of that quadrant's red block size to the source red block size.
- Reflect horizontally for right-side quadrants, vertically for bottom quadrants (both for bottom-right).
- Align the scaled/reflected motif so its red region overlaps the target anchor, then stamp non-bg pixels.

Key insight: Red block size encodes the scale factor; quadrant position encodes the reflection axes.

Input structure:
- Grid divided into NxN cells by separator lines of a single color.

Rule:
- Extract the inner pixel pattern from the minority cell.
- Treat each pixel as a cell-sized stamp: active pixels → minority pattern, inactive → majority pattern.
- Position this scaled-up pattern on the cell grid so existing minority cells align with active pixels.
- Fill in all remaining active positions with the minority pattern.

Key insight: The minority cell's interior is a miniature blueprint of where minority cells should appear at the grid scale — fractal self-similarity.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Extend a green path from one grid edge to the opposite, routing around red bars at a distance dictated by their blue pixel count.

- bg, grey (5) path network, and several small "bordered sprites" each having a border color and a single center pixel of a different color.

- Read the target color set from inside the legend border.
- For each connected component, check whether it contains **all** target colors.

Look up query glyphs in a reference table and mark whether they form a line.

Input structure:
- Teal background with two full-width pink separator rows.
- Above the first separator is a query row of 5x5 glyph cells.
- Between separators is a reference table of the same 5x5 cells; a glyph is
  identified by both its color and its 3x3 shape.

Rule:
- Green-fill the background inside every table cell whose glyph exactly

whether the queried glyphs align as a full row or column in the table.

Input structure:
- bg = 0 (black). A single teal (8) cross centered in the grid.

- Each gap emits a beam of the inner block's color, traveling diagonally outward (direction set by gap position relative to the block).

Repair a one-cell-thick colored line network by replacing singleton markers, filling short orthogonal gaps, and redirecting yellow-marked arms to the edge.

Input structure:

- Assign every marker to the nearest visible line color in row/column line-of-sight, preferring an endpoint supported along that same axis.
- For each line color, fill the gap between consecutive facing endpoints in a row or column.
- A yellow control erases the old straight arm on the far side of its endpoint and paints the same color from that endpoint through the control pixel to the grid edge.

Key insight: The singleton markers identify which sparse stroke fragments belong together; after they are colored, the intended lines are the axis-aligned gaps between facing endpoints, with yellow controls flipping one arm to the marked side.

Extend each colored marker from its directional sprite to a grid edge, painting a dotted ray and the whole edge side.

- If two painted boundary sides meet at a corner, make that shared corner black.

Move each right-side colored shape into the left slot whose template color is its exact complement.

Input structure:
- The grid has two equal-width slots separated by one background column.

- Each band has a shared template color in the left slot and one colored source shape in the right slot.

- For each band, define its destination shape as the cells in the left slot not occupied by the template color.

- Each magenta source can be paired one-to-one with a blue pivot in the same

- Remove all magenta source pixels.
- For each matched source/pivot pair, preserve the source distance from the
  pivot but rotate its offset 90 degrees counterclockwise.
- Paint the rotated in-bounds target orange; if the target is outside the
  grid, the source simply disappears.

unique global matching from each magenta source to its pivot.

references.docstring:

- Each source is an 8-connected component containing a monochrome sprite and one marker pixel of another color.
- Other isolated marker pixels may be destinations; marker colors with no source sprite are distractors.

- Clear the grid to background.
- For every source marker color, place the sprite at each other marker of that color using the source marker as the anchor.
- Keep each destination marker pixel in place; do not keep source sprites, source markers, or distractor markers.

Key insight:
- A colored marker is not part of the sprite geometry; it is the anchor that says where same-colored copies of that sprite should be stamped.

references.docstring:
Move each isolated colored pixel into the one-cell frame around a grey 2x2 block.

Input structure:
- Background is the dominant color.
- Grey foreground objects are solid 2x2 anchor blocks.
- Every other non-background, non-grey cell is a colored singleton source.

Rule:
- Keep the grey anchors fixed and clear all colored singleton source pixels.
- For each singleton and each anchor, the normal destination is the cell reached by
  clamping the pixel into the anchor's one-cell outer frame.
- If a diagonally outside singleton has an exact 8-direction sightline into an anchor,
  also allow the cell just before the first grey pixel on that ray.
- Choose distinct destinations that minimize total king-move distance; at equal
  distance prefer exact sightlines, then the shorter Manhattan movement.

Key insight: The grey 2x2 blocks define magnetic frames; conflicts are resolved
structurally by nearest-frame assignment rather than by color identity.

references.docstring:

- The motif size is 2R+1 by 2C+1, where R by C is the motif lattice size.

- Slots that still contain the repeated motif color map to that repeated motif color.

- The holes and filled odd slots inside one motif are a miniature legend for recoloring the entire repeated motif lattice.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Normalize vertical two-color bars between paired marker columns around the marker rows.

references.docstring:
Crop the foreground object whose missing cells match marker shapes, and fill those missing cells with the marker colors.

Input structure
A dominant background surrounds several monochromatic foreground objects. Exactly one object has background gaps inside its bounding box whose component shapes are matched by separate marker objects.

references.docstring:
Expand the lower color grid by replacing each pixel with its matching top stencil.

Input structure

The legend contains left-to-right 2x2 color swatches and, to their right,

The lower grid is not copied directly; it is an index grid whose colors select

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Move the small colored sprite into the hollow frame by stretching its shape to the frame interior.

references.docstring:
Rotate the colors around every 3x3 foreground ring, with corners and side-centers cycling in opposite directions.

Input structure
- The grid has a dominant background color.
- Each 4-connected foreground object is a complete 3x3 ring: eight foreground pixels around a background center.

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Advance the marker from one half of a vertical bar to the same half of the next longer bar.

Input structure
- The grid has one dominant background color and exactly two foreground colors.

- Each bar's total height encodes an ordered size, and the marker advances from a 2k bar to the corresponding 2(k+1) bar while preserving whether it marks the top or bottom half.

references.docstring:
Slide each blue/teal or yellow/orange row pair together while preserving its left-to-right order.

Input structure
- The grid has a black background.
- Each nonempty row contains exactly two distinct foreground pixels.
- Blue/teal and yellow/orange row pairs are the moving pairs; other color pairs are distractors.

- For each moving pair, keep the left pixel fixed and move the right pixel left until it touches the left pixel.

references.docstring:
Fill the rectangle from the lone foreground pixel to its nearest grid corner.

Input structure

- The foreground pixel's color is the color used for all added pixels.

Rule

- The single pixel is one corner of the rectangle; the opposite corner is the

references.docstring:
Pack the colored sprites along the bottom edge from smallest to largest.

The grid has a dominant background color and several monochrome 4-connected

area from smallest to largest, and paste their bounding-box sprites left to

The original locations do not determine the final slots; each sprite's area
gives the packing order, while its shape and color are preserved.

annotation.dst: pack into the bottom-left corner from smallest to largest by pixel area
annotation.transform: clear original positions; preserve each sprite's shape and color; bottom-align bounding-box sprites with no horizontal gaps

references.docstring:
Transform each 9x9 panel by mirroring across its center guide line or filling all four block slots from its lone exemplar.

guide line.

with a full center row is reflected top-to-bottom. A panel with no guide line

annotation.transform: reflect each guided panel across its guide line; for each unguided panel, recolor all four slots to the slot color that appears only once

references.docstring:
Shift each interior pixel whose color matches a frame side one cell toward that matching side.

Input structure
The grid has a one-cell-thick rectangular frame: the four corners are the
background color, and each side between corners is a solid, distinct side

Interior pixels with the top-side color move one row up, bottom-side color
move one row down, left-side color move one column left, and right-side color
move one column right. A pixel already adjacent to its matching side stays in

The colored frame sides act as direction labels for matching interior pixels.

annotation.path: one orthogonal step toward the same-colored frame side
annotation.trajectory: translate each pixel one cell; pixels already adjacent to their matching side stay in place
annotation.transform: keep the rectangular frame and all non-side-colored interior pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Move the diagonal foreground segment to the next longer run along the same up-right diagonal.

Input structure
The grid has one background color and one foreground color. The foreground pixels form a

Erase the current segment. If its columns are c0..c1 and its length is L, draw the same
color on columns c1+1..c1+L+1 along the same anti-diagonal.

The segment advances past its current upper-right end by one whole segment position, and
the next segment is one pixel longer than the current one.

annotation.path: continue up-right along the same anti-diagonal immediately past the current segment
annotation.trajectory: paint the next contiguous segment one pixel longer than the source
annotation.transform: erase the source segment; keep background unchanged

references.docstring:
Cycle each solid odd-sided square to the next smaller centered square, wrapping a single pixel to a 9x9 square.

Input structure:
- The grid has one dominant background color.
- Every foreground object is a separated 4-connected monochrome solid square.
- Square side lengths are odd and belong to the cycle 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

- Keep each square's color and center.

- The visible operation is on square size, not color: side lengths cycle 1 -> 9 -> 7 -> 5 -> 3 -> 1.

annotation.transform: clear each original square and repaint a centered square of the same color with side length n - 2 when n > 1; a 1x1 object wraps to a centered 9x9 square

references.docstring:

- Each foreground object spans at least two columns in its bounding box.

annotation.transform: for each object, set foreground pixels in its two leftmost bbox columns to bg

references.docstring:
Complete each partially hidden simple foreground shape by recoloring the occluding pixels in its footprint.

annotation.transform: recolor foreground pixels inside each implied shape footprint to that shape's color; leave all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Reflect the solid rectangular source objects across the full separator line and color the gap with the separator color.

annotation.dst: their mirror positions across the separator line

references.docstring:
Move each marked L-shaped sprite onto the separate pixel matching its marker color.

annotation.dst: isolated control pixel d
annotation.match_cond: s.marker.color == d.color and d lies on the outer diagonal ray from s.L_bend through s.marker
annotation.transform: translate s so s.L_bend lands on d; clear original s and consumed d; keep unmatched sprites and unrelated single pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Redraw foreground objects as nested square rings ordered by object size.

Input structure:
- The grid has one dominant background color.
- Every foreground object is a 4-connected monochromatic component.
- Foreground object areas are distinct.

- Sort the foreground objects by decreasing pixel count.
- Create a square output with side length 2 * number_of_objects - 1.

annotation.src: monochromatic foreground objects s ordered by decreasing area
annotation.dst: centered square rings d ordered outside-to-inside
annotation.match_cond: rank(s) == rank(d)
annotation.transform: paint each d with s.color
annotation.grid_shape: square of side 2 * object_count - 1

references.docstring:
Push every colored object touching maroon markers straight outward until it reaches the grid edge.

Input structure:

- Maroon pixels are fixed markers.
- Every other foreground 4-connected object touches the marker pixels on exactly one cardinal side.

- The maroon contact side is a launcher: it determines a unique outward ray for the whole object, and the edge of the grid determines the translation distance.

annotation.path: move straight away from the maroon contact side along the matching row or column
annotation.dst: furthest in-bounds position where the object reaches the grid edge
annotation.trajectory: translate each object once, preserving its shape and color
annotation.transform: clear each moving object from its original position; keep maroon markers unchanged

references.docstring:
Complete sparse nested rectangular color layers into solid rectangles.

The background is the dominant color, and every foreground color marks one
axis-aligned rectangular layer; the layer bboxes have unique areas and are
nested from outermost to innermost.

which already matches at least three sides of its parent's one-pixel inset

The scattered pixels are samples of nested rectangular regions, so the
output is a clean redraw of those regions with inner colors overwriting

annotation.dst: same canvas with each nested rectangular region completed
annotation.transform: infer each color's rectangular layer from its bbox; if a child bbox aligns with its parent's one-pixel-inset interior on at least three sides, expand it to that interior; fill layers from largest to smallest so inner colors overwrite outer colors

references.docstring:

references.docstring:
Extract the single plain rectangle and redraw it with the aligned rectangles' border-relative marker pattern.

references.docstring:
