references.docstring:
Expand the colored runs from the left reference panel into the blank right panel.

Input structure:
- A uniform rectangular frame surrounds the grid.
- One full-height divider of the frame color splits a left reference panel
  from a blank right panel.
- Both panels have one background margin column on each side of their active
  columns; the left active columns contain two-column endpoint slots, possibly
  connected by same-color horizontal runs.

Rule:
- Keep the original grid and paint only in the right panel's active columns.
- A source run exactly matching the left endpoint slot is copied to the left
  two columns of the right active span.
- A source run exactly matching the right endpoint slot is copied to the right
  two columns of the right active span.
- A source run connecting the endpoint slots is stretched across the entire
  right active span.

Key insight:
The left panel is a compressed legend for the right panel: endpoint markers
stay two pixels wide, while connectors between endpoints expand to fill the
distance between them.

annotation.src: colored horizontal runs in the left reference panel's active columns
annotation.dst: blank right panel's active columns
annotation.transform: copy two-column endpoint runs to the corresponding edge of the right active span; stretch any run that connects the endpoint slots across the full active span

references.docstring:
Shift each row's dominant middle-color run left until its right edge aligns with the leftmost original right edge, moving displaced left-side pixels after the run.

Input structure:
- The grid has three colors.
- The most common color forms one contiguous horizontal run in every row.
- Pixels before those runs share one side color, and pixels after those runs share the other side color.

Rule:
- Find the minimum right edge column among the middle-color runs.
- In each row, keep the run width and the trailing right-side color count.
- Place the middle-color run so its right edge is at that minimum column, unless the run is too wide, in which case start it at column 0.
- Fill any remaining non-trailing cells with the left-side color.

Key insight:
The varying row prefixes are movable padding; the stable feature is the leftmost right boundary of the middle-color shape.

annotation.src: dominant middle color forming one contiguous horizontal run in every row, with one left-side color before the runs and one right-side color after them
annotation.transform: shift each middle-color run left so its right edge reaches the minimum original right edge column, or column 0 if the run is wider; move displaced left-side pixels after the run and preserve the right-side suffix

references.docstring:
Repeat each 3x3 control-center sprite toward the matching solid rectangle until a copy first overlaps that rectangle.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- Each sprite is a 3x3 foreground object whose eight border pixels have one color and whose center has a different control color.
- For every control color, there is exactly one separate solid rectangular object of that color.

Rule
- Match each sprite to the unique solid rectangle whose color equals the sprite center.
- Copy the whole 3x3 sprite in the cardinal direction of that rectangle, stepping by three cells each time.
- Stop after pasting the first copy whose 3x3 bbox overlaps the rectangle; copied pixels overwrite the rectangle there.

Key insight
The center pixel is not the paint color: it is a destination key, while the entire 3x3 sprite is the motif tiled along the straight path.

annotation.src: 3x3 sprite s with a uniform border color and a different control-color center
annotation.path: straight cardinal path from s toward d
annotation.trajectory: copy s every three cells until the first copied bbox overlaps d
annotation.dst: separate solid rectangle d whose color matches s.center
annotation.transform: copied sprites overwrite background/rectangle cells; all other input pixels remain unchanged

references.docstring:
Erase the complete interior glyph and expand each endpoint marker pair into its color's full glyph.

Input structure
- The grid is 20x20 with background inside two same-color full-height vertical frame bars.
- Inside the frame there is one complete color glyph and one or more other colors appearing only as two endpoint markers in the same row.
- Marker endpoints are always in the first and last interior columns.

Rule
- Keep the vertical frame unchanged.
- Erase any complete interior glyph.
- For each endpoint marker pair, use that marker color's learned glyph template and anchor its horizontal bar on the marker row.

Key insight
- Color identifies which glyph shape to draw; the two endpoint pixels are not copied objects, they are anchors for reconstructing that color's full symbol.

annotation.src: vertical frame containing one complete color glyph and one or more same-row two-pixel endpoint markers of other colors
annotation.transform: erase the complete glyph; expand each endpoint marker pair into that marker color's learned glyph template anchored on the marker row

references.docstring:
Shift alternating two-color row bars so each row aligns to the topmost bar's color columns.

Input structure:
- The dominant background surrounds horizontal two-pixel bars.
- Every foreground row has exactly one adjacent bar using the same two colors.
- The topmost bar gives the reference left/right column for each color.

Rule:
- Keep bars whose left color is already in its reference column.
- For a reversed bar, shift the whole two-pixel bar horizontally until its
  left color lands in that color's reference column.
- Background cells vacated by shifted bars become background.

Key insight:
- The rows are not recolored; each two-color bar is translated so equal
  colors line up with the topmost reference bar.

annotation.src: two-color horizontal row bar s
annotation.dst: reference color column d established by the topmost row bar
annotation.match_cond: s.left_color == d.color
annotation.transform: translate s horizontally so its left color lands in d; clear vacated cells to background

references.docstring:
Compress the noisy four-region board split by a solid cross into a 3x3 color map.

Input structure:
- A single full row and a single full column have the same solid separator color.
- The separator cross divides the input into four nonempty rectangular regions.
- Each region has a unique dominant color, with other colors acting as noise.

Rule:
- Find the unique solid same-color row/column pair.
- Fill the middle row and middle column of the 3x3 output with the separator color.
- Put the unique dominant color of each quadrant into the corresponding corner.

Key insight:
- The input grid is a noisy enlarged version of the desired 3x3 layout; the cross marks the coarse cell boundaries.

annotation.src: noisy four-region board divided by a solid one-pixel cross
annotation.transform: collapse each quadrant to its unique dominant color and keep the cross color as the middle row and column
annotation.grid_shape: 3x3 coarse color map

references.docstring:
Move each marked cross object away from its marker to the grid edge while rotating the colored cross 180 degrees.

Input structure:
- The background is the dominant color.
- Each 8-connected foreground object has nine pixels: a 4-pixel marker-color
  sprite attached to a 5-pixel non-marker colored cross.
- Each object bbox is either 3x6 or 6x3, so the marker sprite is on exactly
  one side of the cross.

Rule:
- Move the whole object straight away from its marker side until the object
  bbox touches the corresponding grid edge.
- Keep the marker sprite unchanged within the object.
- Rotate the 3x3 colored cross block by 180 degrees before placing it.

Key insight:
The marker sprite is a directional tail; the cross is the leading payload,
and only that payload turns around during the slide to the edge.

annotation.src: each 8-connected composite object made of a 4-pixel blue marker sprite attached to a 5-pixel colored cross
annotation.path: straight away from the marker sprite until the composite bbox reaches the grid edge
annotation.trajectory: move the whole composite rigidly along that path
annotation.transform: rotate the 3x3 colored cross 180 degrees within the composite; keep the marker sprite unchanged

references.docstring:
Repeat the bottom foreground motif upward until it fills the whole grid.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- The only foreground pixels occupy a contiguous block of rows at the bottom.
- That bottom block is the complete vertical motif, including its background cells.

Rule
- Copy the bottom motif rows repeatedly upward across the full grid.
- Preserve horizontal alignment and vertical phase: the original first motif row remains at its input row.
- The output shape is unchanged.

Key insight
The blank rows above the bottom foreground block are missing repetitions of the same row motif, not empty space.

annotation.src: bottom contiguous row motif containing all foreground pixels plus its background cells
annotation.transform: repeat the motif rows upward with the same vertical phase until every row is filled

references.docstring:
Recolor the small defect bars on each shared-color object with the opposite panel color.

Input structure
- The grid contains two large panel colors and one shared object color.
- Each shared-color object is a mostly solid rectangle inside exactly one panel.
Rule
- Find the near-solid rectangular core of each object.
- Missing core pixels and one-cell protrusions define two-pixel bars perpendicular to the nearest core edge.
- Recolor those bars with the other panel color; leave all other pixels unchanged.
Key insight
- The colors to add are not tied to numeric ids: each object's surrounding panel identifies the opposite panel color.

annotation.src: shared-color near-rectangular objects embedded in exactly one of two panel colors
annotation.transform: for each object, find its near-solid rectangular core; recolor two-pixel bars from missing core-edge pixels or one-cell protrusions to the opposite panel color; leave all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Return the ring object reached by following the guide path from the checkerboard object.

Input structure
- The input has one dominant background color, one 3x3 checkerboard object,
  several 3x3 ring objects, and sparse guide pixels on a two-cell lattice.

Rule
- Find the checkerboard object and its unique adjacent guide pixel.
- Follow guide pixels of that color through two-cell horizontal/vertical steps.
- Output the unique 3x3 ring object adjacent to that connected guide path.

Key insight
- The checkerboard object is the source, and the color of its attached guide
  pixel selects the path whose far endpoint points at the answer ring.

annotation.src: the unique 3x3 checkerboard object; its adjacent guide pixel gives the path color
annotation.path: follow same-color guide pixels in horizontal/vertical two-cell steps
annotation.trajectory: path itself is not painted; it selects the ring at the reached endpoint
annotation.dst: the unique 3x3 ring object adjacent to the reached guide path endpoint
annotation.transform: crop and output that ring object unchanged
annotation.grid_shape: input is 22x22; output is the selected 3x3 ring

references.docstring:
Recolor every pixel whose color is not one of the two most frequent input colors to orange.

Input structure:
- The grid contains at least three colors.
- Orange is absent from the input and is used only as the output replacement color.
- Exactly two colors occupy the top two frequency ranks; they may tie with each
  other, but no third color ties them at the cutoff.

Rule:
- Preserve every pixel whose color is one of the two most frequent input colors.
- Replace every other pixel with orange.

Key insight:
- The visible distinction is not the numeric identity of the colors but their
  population: the two majority colors remain, while all minority colors merge
  into the new orange color.

annotation.src: all pixels grouped by input color frequency
annotation.transform: preserve pixels of the two most frequent colors; recolor every pixel of all other colors to orange

references.docstring:
Move the side-attached foreground object to the opposite wall, shear its lower rows inward, and paint the crossed floor cells.

Input structure:
- The top row is the upper background color and the bottom row is the
  floor color.
- A single non-background, non-floor object touches exactly one vertical
  grid edge and rests immediately above the first solid floor row.

Rule:
- Clear the source object to the upper background color.
- Repaint each object row on the opposite side: the first three relative
  rows keep the edge alignment, and each lower row shifts one more pixel
  inward from that side.
- On the first floor row, repaint the traversed side-to-object segment
  maroon, stopping just before the final outer bottom support pixel.

Key insight:
- The side of the source object gives the horizontal direction, while the
  row index inside the object gives the one-cell-per-row diagonal shear.

annotation.src: single grey object attached to one side edge and resting on the pink floor
annotation.path: to the opposite side edge; rows below the first patterned row shift one pixel inward per row
annotation.trajectory: repaint the source object at dst with the diagonal shear
annotation.dst: opposite side edge above the same floor row
annotation.transform: clear source object pixels to blue background; recolor traversed floor segment maroon

references.docstring:
Mark the missing center of each plus-shaped arrangement of four two-pixel bars with yellow.

Input structure:
- The background is the dominant color.
- The single foreground color forms isolated 4-connected objects, each a horizontal or vertical two-pixel bar.
- Some bars form an implied plus sign: two horizontal bars and two vertical bars around an empty center, with a one-pixel gap between the center and each bar.

Rule:
- Keep the input unchanged except at implied plus-sign centers.
- For every background pixel with foreground bars at offsets 2-3 cells left, right, above, and below, recolor that center yellow.
- The one-pixel gaps immediately next to the center in the four cardinal directions must remain background.

Key insight:
- The yellow pixels are not extending a line; they identify the shared missing center where four separated two-pixel bars align as a plus sign.

annotation.src: uniform-background grid of isolated 4-connected two-pixel horizontal and vertical foreground bars
annotation.transform: recolor each background pixel to yellow when it is the center of four aligned two-pixel bars at offsets 2-3 cells left/right/up/down, with one background gap from the center; leave all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Push the central solid rectangle to the grid edge, splitting the perpendicular target rectangle around its path.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- There are exactly three monochrome foreground objects arranged on one
  horizontal or vertical axis.
- The middle object on that axis is a solid rectangular moving object.
- One end object is a solid rectangle or bar whose long side is perpendicular
  to the movement axis; this is the target to split.

Rule
- Move the middle rectangle along the axis toward the target until it is
  flush with the grid edge in that direction.
- Clear the original middle rectangle and the original target.
- Split the target through the moving rectangle's two-cell-wide path and
  shift the two halves one cell outward perpendicular to the movement.
- Keep the other end object unchanged.

Key insight
- The non-target end object acts as a pusher; the central rectangle travels
  away from it through the perpendicular target, opening a matching gap.

annotation.src: middle solid rectangular object between two end objects
annotation.path: straight horizontal or vertical line away from the non-target end object and through the perpendicular solid target rectangle/bar
annotation.dst: place flush with the grid edge beyond the target
annotation.trajectory: paint only the final moved rectangle at dst
annotation.transform: erase original source pixels; split the target rectangle/bar along the moving object's two-cell-wide path and shift its two halves one cell outward perpendicular to the movement; keep the other end object unchanged

references.docstring:
Erase the first border pixel hit by extending the red marker away from its pink trail.

Input structure
- The dominant background surrounds a unique red marker and a four-pixel
  pink trail.
- The pink pixels form one straight 8-connected ray starting next to the
  red marker.
- In the opposite direction from that trail, the red marker faces a
  non-background border or obstacle pixel beyond background cells.

Rule
- Keep the whole grid fixed except for the first non-background pixel on
  the ray from the red marker away from the pink trail.
- Recolor that one hit pixel to the background color.

Key insight
- The pink trail marks where the red marker came from, so the edit is found
  by ray-casting from the red marker in the opposite direction.

annotation.src: red marker with a four-pixel pink trail
annotation.path: ray from the red marker away from the pink trail until the first non-background pixel
annotation.trajectory: ray itself is not painted; it selects the first hit pixel
annotation.dst: first border or obstacle pixel hit by the ray
annotation.transform: recolor the hit pixel to background; keep all other pixels unchanged

references.docstring:
Recolor each non-singleton red object by its symmetry axis and erase isolated red pixels.

Input structure:
- The grid has one dominant background color and red 4-connected foreground objects.
- Every non-singleton red object has exactly one reflection symmetry category:
  horizontal, vertical, or diagonal.
- Single red pixels are noise.

Rule:
- Start from an all-background output of the same shape.
- Recolor horizontally symmetric red objects blue, vertically symmetric objects
  green, and diagonally symmetric objects pink.
- Leave isolated red pixels as background.

Key insight: The target color is not tied to object position or size; it is a
label for the object's reflection symmetry.

annotation.src: red 4-connected objects on a dominant background, including singleton noise pixels
annotation.transform: delete singleton red pixels; recolor each larger object in place by its reflection symmetry: horizontal blue, vertical green, diagonal pink

references.docstring:
Compress the stacked colored bars into a compact ordered table with the control pixel on the selected row.

Input structure
- A background grid contains several full-width colored bars from top to
  bottom; the last bar is the base/separator color.
- Each non-base bar may have an aligned three-column comb motif below it,
  alternating side-pair rows with solid rows.
- A singleton control pixel sits away from the colored motifs.

Rule
- Make one output row per non-base bar, preserving top-to-bottom order.
- In that row, paint the bar color once for each solid three-pixel row in
  its motif, then paint the base-bar color in the separator column.
- The singleton control pixel sits immediately above the base bar. Among
  motifs whose open side-pair parity is compatible with that bottom row,
  put the control pixel in the output row with the fewest solid rows; use
  horizontal distance to the motif center only to break count ties.

Key insight
- The vertical comb height is a count, while the control pixel is read by
  projecting it onto the center gap of compatible comb rows rather than by
  its vertical band alone.

annotation.src: full-width colored bars with aligned three-column comb motifs; the final full-width bar is the separator color
annotation.dst: compact rows in the same top-to-bottom bar order
annotation.transform: paint each row with the bar color repeated once per solid motif row, append the separator color column, and place the singleton control pixel on the row whose open motif center is nearest to it
annotation.multi_step: top-to-bottom order breaks equal marker-center distances
annotation.grid_shape: one row per non-separator bar; columns are count slots plus separator and control-pixel columns

references.docstring:
Extend each solid foreground rectangle toward its same-color isolated pixels with capped one-cell paths, clearing each original marker pixel.

Input structure
- The background is the dominant color.
- Each foreground color has exactly one solid rectangular object and one or more isolated same-color marker pixels.
- Every marker is horizontally or vertically aligned with the rectangle bbox and lies outside it.
Rule
- For each marker, draw a one-cell-wide straight path from the adjacent side of the rectangle through one cell beyond the marker.
- Add a three-pixel perpendicular cap at the rectangle end and around the marker endpoint.
- Recolor the original marker pixel to background.
Key insight
- The isolated pixels are not copied; they mark the hollow endpoints of capped protrusions grown from their matching rectangle.

annotation.src: solid foreground rectangles and same-color isolated marker pixels
annotation.path: straight horizontal or vertical path from the aligned rectangle side to one cell beyond each marker
annotation.trajectory: paint a one-cell-wide path with three-pixel perpendicular caps at the rectangle side and marker endpoint
annotation.transform: clear each original marker pixel to background; keep the rectangles unchanged

references.docstring:
Add the two missing colored arms of a centered diamond-sprite motif, or clear a completed motif to a blank square.

Input structure
An 11x11 board has orange background and pink separator bars forming nine 3x3 cells. Occupied cells contain a four-pixel diamond sprite; the center cell and one neighboring cell are red, and a completed board may also contain one grey and one teal sprite.

Rule
With only the two red sprites present, preserve the board and add grey and teal diamond sprites 135 degrees clockwise and counterclockwise from the non-center red arm. If those expected grey and teal sprites are already present, output an all-background square whose side length is the total number of sprite pixels.

Key insight
The non-center red sprite is an eight-neighbor direction from the center; the other two colored arms are fixed rotations of that direction.

annotation.src: 3x3 cell board with a red center diamond sprite and one red neighboring diamond sprite
annotation.dst: the two rotated arm cells of the centered motif
annotation.transform: add a grey sprite 135 degrees clockwise and a teal sprite 135 degrees counterclockwise from the red arm around the center; if both are already present, erase to an all-background 16x16 square
annotation.grid_shape: same for the adding step; completed motif becomes 16x16

references.docstring:
Extract the lattice subregion bounded by the four background-colored corner holes.

Input structure:
- A regular one-cell-thick lattice has one line color, one background color,
  and sparse marker pixels.
- Exactly four lattice-line intersections are background-colored holes instead
  of line-color pixels.

Rule:
- Find the unique non-background color that forms regular horizontal and
  vertical lattice lines.
- Use the four background-colored lattice intersections as the corners of one
  rectangle.
- Return the inclusive crop between those corner rows and columns.

Key insight:
- The crop is marked by the missing lattice intersections, not by the marker
  pixels inside the cells.

annotation.src: regular one-cell-thick lattice with exactly four background-colored holes at lattice intersections
annotation.transform: output the inclusive rectangular crop whose four corners are those holes; preserve all pixels inside the region
annotation.grid_shape: crop to the hole-corner rectangle

references.docstring:
Extract the top-left or top-right 2x2 corner crop selected by the top edge clue.

Input structure
- The input is a square color grid whose answer is one of the two 2x2 crops
  touching the top edge and a grid corner.
- A repeated color on the top row, when present, acts as the primary side cue.
- Otherwise, the two top corner colors have different whole-grid frequencies.

Rule
- If a top-row color repeats, find the repeated top-row occurrence nearest to
  a left or right edge and take the 2x2 top-corner crop on that side.
- If the top row has no repeated color, compare the whole-grid frequencies of
  the two top-corner colors and take the side whose corner color is rarer.

Key insight
- The task is not asking for an arbitrary 2x2 search: the decisive information
  is on the top edge, and it selects which top corner crop to keep.

annotation.src: top edge of the square color grid, using repeated top-row colors or the two top corner colors
annotation.dst: the 2x2 crop touching the top edge and the selected grid corner
annotation.transform: if a top-row color repeats, crop the top corner nearest to the closest repeated occurrence; otherwise crop the side whose top-corner color is rarer in the full grid

references.docstring:
Fill each black 5x5 region's missing interior positions with a fixed 3x3 positional color legend.

Input structure
- The grid uses teal as the dominant background and black for one or more
  5x5 regions.
- Each black region has a black one-pixel border and a 3x3 interior that
  may already contain teal pixels.

Rule
- Overlay the legend 1 7 6 / 4 8 5 / 2 9 3 on the 3x3 interior of every
  5x5 black region.
- Wherever an interior non-center legend position is still black, recolor it
  to the corresponding legend color; leave existing teal pixels, the center,
  and the black border unchanged.

Key insight
- The colored output pixels are not derived from the teal motif shape; they
  are the fixed position labels for the missing cells of each 3x3 interior.

annotation.src: black 5x5 regions on teal background, each with a 3x3 interior containing some teal pixels
annotation.transform: overlay the fixed positional legend 1 7 6 / 4 8 5 / 2 9 3 on each 3x3 interior; recolor black non-center interior pixels to their legend color and leave teal pixels and borders unchanged

references.docstring:
Replace the outlined object with the outside contour of that outline in the marker color.

Input structure:
- A dominant background surrounds one 8-connected foreground outline.
- The outline is the unique largest foreground color.
- One or more smaller interior colors are inside the outline; the marker color
  is the unique smallest non-outline color.

Rule:
- Erase all original foreground pixels to background.
- Paint every background pixel that is 4-adjacent to the outline with the
  marker color.
- Keep the grid shape unchanged.

Key insight: The colored interior marker supplies the paint color, while the
largest outline supplies only the contour whose outside edge is traced.

annotation.src: one 8-connected largest foreground outline object and smaller interior marker colors on a dominant background
annotation.transform: erase all original foreground pixels; repaint the background pixels 4-adjacent to the outline with the unique smallest non-outline marker color

references.docstring:
Convert scattered foreground objects into bottom-aligned count bars in a fixed five-color order.

Input structure
The grid has a dominant background color and foreground objects in the task
palette: grey, red, teal, maroon, and pink. Objects are monochromatic
8-connected components; some palette colors may be absent.

Rule
For each palette color in order grey, red, teal, maroon, pink, count its
8-connected objects. Create a background grid with five columns and height
equal to the largest count, then fill each column upward from the bottom
with its palette color for that count.

Key insight
The output does not preserve object shapes or positions; it is a histogram
of per-color 8-connected object counts, using the learned palette order.

annotation.src: monochromatic foreground objects using 8-connectivity, grouped by color
annotation.dst: bottom-aligned histogram columns in fixed palette order: grey, red, teal, maroon, pink
annotation.transform: count the 8-connected objects of each palette color and fill that many cells upward from the bottom of its column
annotation.grid_shape: height is the largest color object count; width is five palette columns

references.docstring:
Replace an orange canvas with concentric Manhattan-distance color rings centered on the lone marker pixel.

Input structure:
- The grid is an orange background with exactly one non-orange marker pixel.
- The marker color is one of the colors in the fixed non-orange ring cycle.

Rule:
- The marker location is distance 0 and keeps the marker color.
- Each step of Manhattan distance away from the marker advances one position
  through the cycle green, yellow, black, grey, red, teal, maroon, pink, blue.
- Fill every pixel of the original grid by this distance-indexed cycle.

Key insight: The output is not copied from existing objects; it is the
distance field around the single marker, colored by a cyclic palette that
excludes the orange background.

annotation.src: single non-orange marker pixel on an orange background
annotation.dst: entire grid as concentric Manhattan-distance rings centered on the marker
annotation.transform: use the marker color at distance 0, then advance one step per Manhattan distance through the fixed cycle green, yellow, black, grey, red, teal, maroon, pink, blue

references.docstring:
Recover the repeating background pattern hidden under the largest solid rectangle.

Input structure:
- The grid is covered by a small row/column periodic pattern.
- Several non-pattern colors form solid rectangular foreground objects that
  overwrite the pattern.
- The requested output region is the largest of those solid rectangles.

Rule:
- Find every 4-connected monochromatic object whose bounding box is a filled
  rectangle with both dimensions greater than one.
- Treat those rectangles as masks, infer the smallest repeating tile that is
  consistent with all remaining visible pixels, and repaint the largest
  rectangle's coordinates with that tile.

Key insight: The rectangle colors are occluders; the visible pixels outside
them are enough to reconstruct the original periodic background underneath.

annotation.src: visible periodic background outside the solid rectangular occluders
annotation.dst: region covered by the largest solid rectangular occluder
annotation.transform: infer the minimal repeating tile from unoccluded pixels and output the tile values that would occupy the largest rectangle's coordinates
annotation.grid_shape: same shape as the largest rectangle

references.docstring:
Fill each centered square ring with the color of the marker at that ring distance.

Input structure
The input is an odd square grid with a dominant background color and one
non-background marker for every Chebyshev distance from the grid center.
Rule
The output replaces the background with concentric square rings centered on
the middle cell; every cell at distance d from the center takes the color of
the unique marker whose distance from the center is d.
Key insight
The scattered markers are not objects to move; their Chebyshev distances
form a palette for the centered square rings.

annotation.src: non-background marker pixel s
annotation.dst: centered square ring region d
annotation.match_cond: s.chebyshev_distance_to_grid_center == d.ring_radius
annotation.transform: fill every pixel in d with s.color

references.docstring:
Summarize the enclosed table slots by the single object color inside each slot, using the slot background color for empty slots.

Input structure
- The most common color forms the outer background and all enclosed slot
  backgrounds.
- The enclosed background components form a complete rectangular array of
  slots, ordered by their positions.
- Each slot contains either no other color or exactly one object color.

Rule
- Find all 4-connected components of the most common color that do not touch
  the input edge.
- Sort their bounding boxes into row and column order to define the output
  table.
- For each slot, output its unique non-background color if present; otherwise
  output the background color.

Key insight
- The large grid is an expanded table: the enclosed background components are
  the cells, and any colored object drawn inside a cell is that cell's summary
  value.

annotation.src: enclosed 4-connected background-color slot components arranged as a rectangular table, each containing zero or one non-background object color
annotation.transform: collapse each slot to one output pixel in row/column order: use the contained object color if present, otherwise use the background color
annotation.grid_shape: number of slot rows x number of slot columns

references.docstring:
Recolor each framed interior mask with the color from the next red frame clockwise around the blue connector cycle.

Input structure
- The grid contains hollow red square frames connected pairwise by blue line components.
- The blue components connect the frames into one cycle, with every frame touching exactly two blue components.
- Each frame interior contains background plus exactly one non-background color mask.

Rule
- Sort the red frames clockwise by their centers around the cycle.
- Keep each frame's interior mask shape in place, but recolor it with the interior color from the next clockwise frame.
- Leave the red frames, blue connectors, background, and interior background holes unchanged.

Key insight
- The colored masks do not move; the blue cycle gives the order in which their colors rotate.

annotation.src: the unique non-background interior color of each red frame, with frames ordered clockwise around the blue connector cycle
annotation.dst: the interior foreground mask of each red frame in the same clockwise frame order
annotation.match_cond: source color at clockwise rank k recolors destination mask at rank k-1, wrapping around the cycle
annotation.transform: recolor each destination mask in place; keep mask shapes, frame borders, blue connectors, and background unchanged

references.docstring:

annotation.match_cond: rank(s) == rank(d) after applying the block-order rule
annotation.transform: copy each whole source block unchanged into its assigned output slot
annotation.multi_step: default order is a one-block left shift; if adjacent shared-color marker rows read the current block colors right-to-left, use reverse order

references.docstring:
Paint the top-connected middle channel between two orange path components teal.

Input structure
- The background is black.
- One foreground color forms exactly two 4-connected one-pixel-wide path components.
- Optional non-background control pixels may sit in the channel between the two paths.

Rule
- Dilate each path component by one cell in the 8-neighborhood and intersect the two dilations; this gives the one-cell-wide middle channel.
- A control pixel in that channel is a blocker only when its 4-neighbors touch fewer than both path components; otherwise it is part of the channel and is repainted.
- After removing blockers, paint the channel component connected to the top edge teal and keep all other pixels unchanged.

Key insight
- The desired pixels are not found by region filling; they are the geometric overlap of the two paths' one-cell halos, with weakly attached control pixels splitting the channel.

annotation.src: middle-channel mask formed by intersecting the 8-neighborhood halos of the two orange 4-connected path objects
annotation.transform: recolor the top-connected passable channel to teal; a non-bg control pixel blocks the channel only if it is not 4-adjacent to both orange path objects, otherwise it is recolored too

references.docstring:
Compress each colored ray pixel inward until it touches that color's 3x3 anchor block.
Input structure
- A uniform background grid with non-background colors.
- Each foreground color contains one solid 3x3 anchor block; all other pixels of that color lie on straight 8-neighbor rays aimed at that block.
Rule
- Keep anchor blocks fixed, erase loose foreground pixels, and for each ray pack its pixels into consecutive cells adjacent to the anchor along the same ray.
Key insight
- The scattered pixels are displaced pixels on visible row, column, or diagonal sightlines back to their same-colored 3x3 block.

annotation.src: loose non-background pixels outside each same-colored solid 3x3 anchor block
annotation.path: straight horizontal, vertical, or diagonal ray from each loose pixel toward its anchor block, stopping at the cell just before the ray enters the anchor
annotation.trajectory: pack all loose pixels on the same ray into consecutive cells adjacent to the anchor, preserving their order by distance from the anchor
annotation.transform: keep the 3x3 anchor blocks fixed, erase the original loose pixels, and preserve each color's pixel count

references.docstring:
Reorient each two-pixel blue/pink segment so it reads pink then blue when viewed from its border marker.

Input structure
- The background is dominant, with one border-only marker color and blue/pink foreground segments.
- Every marker lies on the outer border and points inward along its row or column.
- Along exactly one inward ray from each marker is a single adjacent two-pixel blue/pink segment.

Rule
- For each marker, look inward perpendicular to the border side containing the marker.
- Rewrite the two blue/pink pixels on that ray so the nearer one is pink and the farther one is blue.
- Keep marker pixels, background pixels, and all other pixels unchanged.

Key insight
- The marker gives a local viewing direction; the segment's required order is relative to that marker, not to global row or column order.

annotation.src: border marker pixel s
annotation.dst: adjacent blue/pink segment d on an inward row or column ray
annotation.match_cond: d lies on the unique inward ray from s
annotation.transform: rewrite d so the pixel nearer s is pink and the farther pixel is blue

references.docstring:
Build the woven rectangle determined by the two marked cells on each crossed bar.

Input structure
A black-background grid contains one long horizontal bar and one long vertical bar.
Each bar has a dominant base color and exactly two same-colored marker pixels.

Rule
The horizontal marker pair gives the output column span.  From the horizontal bar
row, walk toward the farther vertical marker; rows and columns alternate every
other cell.  Even step/even offset cells use the horizontal marker color until
the nearer vertical marker is reached, then use the vertical marker color.
Odd row steps use the horizontal base on marker columns and the original
crossing color on spacer columns.  Spacer columns on even row steps use the
vertical base, except at the switch row where they use the crossing color.

Key insight
The original cross cell records which base color wins at base/base lattice
crossings; the nearer vertical marker is the color-switch boundary.

annotation.src: one horizontal bar and one vertical bar crossing on the background; each bar has a dominant base color and exactly two same-colored marker pixels
annotation.transform: replace the scene with the woven rectangle whose columns span the horizontal marker pair and whose rows run from the horizontal bar to the farther vertical marker; alternate rows and columns every other cell, switch marker color at the nearer vertical marker, and use the original crossing color at base/base lattice intersections

references.docstring:
Complete every colored sprite by applying the union of all aligned partial sprite masks.

Input structure:
- The dominant color is the background.
- Each non-background color appears as a separated partial copy of one common sprite mask.
- The copies share a top-left-aligned sprite window; some copies may be missing lower or right edge pixels.

Rule:
- Crop each same-color mask to its bounding box.
- Pad the crops to the maximum observed height and width, aligned at the top-left, and OR them into one complete template.
- Fill that template at every sprite location using the sprite's own color.

Key insight:
- No single input sprite is complete, but their missing cells are complementary, so the aligned union reveals the full mask.

annotation.src: same-color partial sprite masks, one per foreground color, sharing a top-left-aligned window
annotation.transform: pad smaller masks down/right to the largest observed window, recover the complete sprite as the union of all aligned masks, then fill that mask in each sprite window using that window's color

references.docstring:
Connect same-colored foreground components with one-cell-wide orthogonal paths around teal wall segments.

Input structure
- The dominant color is the background.
- Teal cells are fixed wall segments and are never source connectors.
- Other foreground colors appear as one or more 4-connected components; colors with a single component stay unchanged.

Rule
- For each non-background, non-teal color, read its 4-connected components in row-major order.
- Connect each consecutive pair by the shortest clear L-shaped path between the two components.
- Clear paths may pass only through background or the same color, and they preserve the previous travel axis when both bends are possible.

Key insight
- The output is not a global recolor: each color traces a routed chain through its own components while teal cells and other colors act as blockers.

annotation.src: non-background, non-teal colors with multiple 4-connected components
annotation.path: from each component to the next same-colored component in row-major order, take a shortest clear one-bend horizontal/vertical path through background or same color; teal wall segments and other colors block the path
annotation.dst: next same-colored component in the ordered chain
annotation.trajectory: paint every background pixel on each connector path with the source color
annotation.transform: keep teal wall segments, single-component colors, and all original foreground pixels unchanged
annotation.multi_step: process each color's components in row-major order; when both bends are clear, preserve the previous travel axis, otherwise use the longer-axis-first clear bend

references.docstring:
Crop out the grid half containing the two aligned marker pixels, then erase the markers to background.

Input structure
- The grid has a dominant background color and one non-background marker color
  that appears as exactly two cells.
- The marker cells are aligned either in one row or one column and both lie
  in the same half along that direction.
- Other non-background pixels are content inside one or both halves.

Rule
- If the markers share a row, keep the left or right half whose columns
  contain them.
- If the markers share a column, keep the top or bottom half whose rows
  contain them.
- In the kept half, recolor the marker pixels to the background color.

Key insight
- The two marker pixels are not part of the picture; their alignment and
  half-position identify which half of the doubled canvas is the answer.

annotation.src: half-grid region containing the two aligned marker pixels
annotation.transform: crop to that half; use row-aligned markers to choose left/right and column-aligned markers to choose top/bottom, then recolor marker pixels to bg
annotation.grid_shape: same height and half width for row-aligned markers; half height and same width for column-aligned markers

references.docstring:
Move the orange rectangle onto the maroon rectangle and mark gated corridor crossings in red.

Input structure
- The dominant background contains black obstacle segments.
- There is one solid orange rectangle and one solid maroon rectangle of the same size.
- The two rectangles share either their row span or their column span, so the move is straight and axis-aligned.

Rule
- Erase the original orange rectangle to the background.
- Replace the maroon rectangle with the orange rectangle.
- Between the two rectangles, paint red across the moving rectangle's width or height only at corridor cells flanked by black obstacle segments perpendicular to the movement.

Key insight
- The black segments define gates in the straight corridor; only those gated openings, not every swept background cell, become red.

annotation.src: solid orange rectangle s
annotation.path: straight horizontal or vertical corridor from s to the aligned same-sized maroon rectangle d
annotation.dst: same-sized maroon rectangle d aligned with s on one axis
annotation.trajectory: paint red only at corridor openings flanked by black segments perpendicular to the path
annotation.transform: erase old s to background; replace d with orange; keep black segments and all other cells unchanged

references.docstring:
Split the two-color object horizontally, swap its colors, and slide the upper half to the right.

Input structure:
- The grid has one background color and exactly two foreground colors.
- All foreground pixels form one 4-connected object with an even-height bbox.
- The object has foreground pixels on both rows adjacent to its horizontal midpoint.

Rule:
- Split the object into upper and lower halves at the midpoint of its bbox.
- Swap the two foreground colors in both halves.
- Keep the lower half in place and shift the upper half right until its lower-left
  boundary pixel is diagonally adjacent to the lower half's upper-right boundary pixel.

Key insight:
- The object is not copied or reflected; it is broken at the horizontal waist,
  recolored by exchanging the two visible object colors, then rejoined diagonally.

annotation.src: upper half s of the single two-color foreground object split at its horizontal midpoint
annotation.path: translate s right until its bottom-row leftmost foreground pixel is diagonally adjacent to the lower half's top-row rightmost foreground pixel
annotation.trajectory: place only the final translated upper-half sprite; leave no trail
annotation.dst: endpoint beside the fixed lower half
annotation.transform: exchange the two foreground colors in both halves; keep the lower half in place and clear the original upper-half cells

references.docstring:
Replace each colored corner marker with its corner-specific inward stencil in the same color.

Input structure
- The grid is 8x8 with a single dominant background color.
- Foreground pixels are marker pixels, each located at one of the four corners.
- A marker's color is carried to the stencil selected by its corner position.

Rule
- Erase each corner marker back to the background.
- Top corner markers become an inward 2x2 block one cell away from the top and side edges.
- Bottom corner markers become the mirrored three-pixel inward bent stencil shown by the bottom-corner examples.

Key insight
- The marker position selects the fixed stencil; the marker color only supplies the paint color, so multiple corners apply independently.

annotation.src: colored marker pixels at the four corners of the 8x8 grid
annotation.transform: erase each marker and stamp its color into the fixed inward stencil for that corner: top corners become 2x2 blocks, bottom corners become mirrored three-pixel bent stencils

references.docstring:
Move the left-edge fragment into its same-colored anchor fragment to complete a solid rectangle.

Input structure
- The grid has a dominant background color.
- Exactly one foreground color is split into two 4-connected objects: one
  touches the left edge, and the other is an anchor away from the left edge.
- The translated left-edge object and the anchor can form one filled rectangle.
Rule
- Find the unique split color whose left-edge object can be translated onto
  background cells beside the other same-colored object so their union is a
  solid axis-aligned rectangle.
- Clear the left-edge object's original cells to the background.
- Paint that object at the unique completing offset, preserving all other cells.
Key insight
- The active color is identified by object structure and rectangle completion,
  not by a fixed color id; the same-colored anchor object stays in place.

annotation.src: left-edge 4-connected object s of the split foreground color
annotation.dst: same-colored anchor object d away from the left edge
annotation.match_cond: s.color == d.color and a translation of s plus d forms a filled axis-aligned rectangle
annotation.transform: erase s from its original cells and translate it to the unique completing offset; preserve d and all other cells

references.docstring:
Select the majority interior marker color, then redraw the framed board as that color's frame plus its bounding-box outline.

Input structure:
- The top row is a copied palette made from adjacent equal color pairs.
- Below it is a one-cell-thick rectangular frame around a black interior.
- Non-black, non-frame interior pixels are marker colors; one marker color has
  the unique highest count.

Rule:
- Keep the palette row unchanged.
- Pick the uniquely most frequent interior marker color.
- Clear the lower board to black, recolor its outer frame with the picked color,
  and draw the picked color's interior bounding-box border.

Key insight:
- The noisy marker cloud is not preserved as pixels; only the majority marker
  color and its spatial extent define the output.

annotation.src: framed lower region with black background and colored interior marker pixels
annotation.transform: copy the palette row; select the unique most frequent marker color, clear the lower region to black, recolor the outer frame, and draw that color's bbox border
